analogy.p: A formula is like a present wrapped in layers: y = 3x + 5 means x was first multiplied by 3 (wrapped in paper) and then had 5 added (a ribbon tied on top). To get the present (x) out, you must remove the ribbon first (subtract 5) and then the paper (divide by 3), in the reverse order of wrapping. This shows why the order of undoing matters. It breaks down because a real parcel only has one way to unwrap, whereas in algebra when the subject appears twice you must first gather the pieces together by factorising.

bullets: A **formula** links two or more variables (letters) with an equals sign, for example A = πr² or v = u + at; an **equation** is solved for numbers, whereas a formula is **rearranged** for a letter.
The **subject** is the letter that stands alone with coefficient 1 on one side; everything else sits on the other side.
Rearranging is exactly the same skill as solving an equation, except that you are left with letters (not a number) on the other side.
You must **never** substitute numbers first unless the question says so; the method marks are for the rearrangement in letters.
The answer must show the new subject alone, e.g. **t = (v − u)/a**, not t × a = v − u.
If a question says 'make x the subject', x must appear **once**, only on one side, and **not** inside the other side as well.
Equivalent final forms are accepted (for example x = (v − u)/a or x = v/a − u/a), but a fully simplified single fraction is safest.
core.p: The **subject** of a formula is the single letter on its own on one side of the equals sign, usually on the left, such as **v** in v = u + at. **Rearranging a formula** (also called **changing the subject**) means rewriting it so that a different letter is on its own, for example t = (v − u)/a. The Edexcel specification asks you to rearrange formulae to change the subject, including cases where the subject appears **twice**, or where a **power or root** of the subject appears. The formula says exactly the same thing before and after; only the arrangement changes. This matters because in real problems the quantity you are asked for is rarely the one the formula was written for.

bullets: **Inverse pairs**: + and −, × and ÷, square and square root, cube and cube root, reciprocal (1/x) and reciprocal.
Work out the **order of operations on the subject** (BIDMAS), then undo it in the **reverse** order: first undo + and −, then × and ÷, then powers and roots.
Do the **same thing to every term** on the other side: if you divide by 3 the whole of the right-hand side must be divided by 3, e.g. y = 3x + 5 gives (y − 5)/3, not y − 5/3.
Write each step on a **new line** with the equals signs underneath each other so the examiner can award **method marks**.
A negative coefficient is dealt with by dividing by the negative: −2x = 8 gives x = −4, so a − b = c can be written as −b = c − a, so b = a − c.
You may swap the two sides of the equation at the end to put the subject on the left; this is allowed because equality is symmetrical.
Check with numbers: pick easy values, work out the original, then see if the rearranged formula returns your starting number.
core.h: The balance principle and inverse operations
core.p: Rearranging works because an equation is like a pair of **balanced scales**: whatever you do to one side you must do to the **whole** of the other side. To get the subject on its own you **undo** each operation attached to it using its **inverse operation**: the inverse of adding is subtracting, of multiplying is dividing, of squaring is square rooting, and of cubing is cube rooting. You undo in the **reverse order** to the order in which the operations were applied to the subject, so the last operation applied is the first one you undo. A helpful picture is that the letter is wrapped in layers, like a parcel, and you unwrap from the outside in.

bullets: y = mx + c, make x the subject: subtract c to get y − c = mx, then divide by m to get **x = (y − c)/m**.
P = 2l + 2w, make l the subject: P − 2w = 2l, so **l = (P − 2w)/2** (or l = P/2 − w).
F = 9C/5 + 32, make C the subject: F − 32 = 9C/5, multiply by 5 to get 5(F − 32) = 9C, divide by 9 to get **C = 5(F − 32)/9**.
v = u + at, make a the subject: v − u = at, so **a = (v − u)/t**.
A = ½(a + b)h, make b the subject: 2A = (a + b)h, so 2A/h = a + b, so **b = 2A/h − a**.
When fractions are present, **multiply through** to clear them first, since that reduces the chance of an error.
After each rearrangement, use quick **substitution of simple numbers** to check (for example u = 2, a = 3, t = 4 gives v = 14, and (14 − 2)/3 = 4 ✓).
core.p: The simplest formulae need only one or two inverse operations. In v = u + at, to make **u** the subject you subtract at from both sides to get u = v − at, which is a one-step change. To make **t** the subject you first subtract u from both sides to get at = v − u, then divide both sides by a, giving **t = (v − u)/a**. The key idea is that **at** is a single term (a multiplied by t), so you must divide the **whole** side by a, not just the v. Marks are lost most often by dividing only part of the expression, so always put brackets round the whole of the numerator.

bullets: Check that last answer with x = 1: y = 5 × 3 + 3 = 18, then (18 − 8)/10 = 1 ✓.
Expanding is **required** if the subject also appears outside the bracket, such as y = 3(x + 2) + x.
The number multiplying a bracket applies to **every term inside**; so −2(x − 4) = −2x + 8 (watch the sign!).
A bracket raised to a power, such as y = (x + 1)², is undone by **square rooting both sides**, remembering ± (see later section).
Never 'cancel' a term from the top of a fraction with a term from the bottom unless it is a common **factor** of the whole numerator.
core.p: When the subject sits inside a bracket there are two legitimate routes, and a top student knows both. Take y = 4(x − 3). You can **divide both sides by 4** first, giving y/4 = x − 3, then add 3 to get **x = y/4 + 3**. Alternatively you can **expand** the bracket to get y = 4x − 12, then add 12 and divide by 4 to get x = (y + 12)/4. Both are correct and they are equivalent, because y/4 + 3 = (y + 12)/4. Dividing first is usually faster when the bracket multiplies the whole of the other side as a single factor, and expanding is necessary when the bracket is joined to other terms.

bullets: y = k/x: ×x → xy = k → ÷y → **x = k/y**.
a/b = c/d, make b the subject: cross-multiply to get ad = bc, so **b = ad/c**.
R = V/I, make I the subject: RI = V, so **I = V/R** (a very common physics rearrangement).
1/f = 1/u + 1/v, make v the subject: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = (u − f)/(fu), so **v = fu/(u − f)** (take the reciprocal of both sides only after combining into a single fraction).
Never take the reciprocal term by term: if 1/v = 1/f − 1/u, it is **wrong** to write v = f − u.
If there are fractions with different denominators, multiply through by the **lowest common multiple** of the denominators to clear all of them at once.
core.p: If the subject is on the bottom of a fraction, you must bring it out of the denominator by **multiplying both sides by that denominator**. In y = k/x, multiply both sides by x to get xy = k, then divide both sides by y to get **x = k/y**. The common mistake is to think the answer is x = y/k; the reciprocal relationship means the answer has k on top. For fractions with several terms, multiply **every term** by the denominator, and when two fractions are equal you can **cross-multiply**, which means multiplying each numerator by the other denominator. This is the same as multiplying both sides by both denominators.

bullets: A = πr²: ÷π → r² = A/π → **r = √(A/π)** (radius is positive, so no ± is needed).
y = x² + 3: subtract 3 → x² = y − 3 → **x = ±√(y − 3)**.
y = √(x − 4): square both sides → y² = x − 4 → **x = y² + 4**.
E = ½mv², make v the subject: 2E = mv² → 2E/m = v² → **v = √(2E/m)**.
y = (x + 1)²: **x = ±√y − 1**, with the −1 outside the root because you subtract 1 after square rooting.
Be careful: √(a + b) is **not** √a + √b, and you cannot square root term by term.
Cube roots work the same way: V = x³ gives **x = ∛V**, and a cube root has only one real answer (no ±).
core.h: Formulae with squares and square roots
core.p: If the subject is squared you undo it by **square rooting both sides**, and if the subject is inside a square root you undo it by **squaring both sides**. For example, in A = πr² you divide by π to get r² = A/π and then square root to get **r = √(A/π)**. For a pure equation such as x² = 9 there are two answers, x = +3 and x = −3, which is written **x = ±3**. In a formula about a real length or radius the negative root is usually rejected, but if the question just says 'make x the subject' of something like y = x² you should show the **±** unless context says the quantity is positive. Always undo the other operations first (add, subtract, multiply, divide) before squaring or square rooting, so that you operate on the **whole** side.

bullets: ax + b = cx + d: collect → ax − cx = d − b → factorise → x(a − c) = d − b → **x = (d − b)/(a − c)**.
Expand brackets **before** collecting terms: the subject may be hiding inside a bracket.
Keep the subject terms on the side where they are **positive** if you can; it makes the factorising neater, but either side is correct.
In the factorised form x(y − 2) the bracket (y − 2) must be divided as a **whole**, so write ÷ (y − 2), never ÷ y and ÷ 2 separately.
If your final bracket could be zero, the formula is undefined for that value; this is not usually examined at GCSE but shows understanding.
core.h: When the subject appears twice: collect and factorise (Higher)
core.p: The hardest rearrangements, and a regular 4 or 5 mark Higher question, have the subject in **more than one place**, such as y = (2x + 1)/(x − 3) or ax + b = cx + d. You cannot isolate x by simply undoing operations because x is trapped in two terms. The solution has a fixed **four-stage method**: (1) clear fractions and brackets, (2) get every term containing the subject on **one side** and every other term on the other side, (3) **factorise** the subject out as a common factor, and (4) **divide** by the bracket that remains. The factorising step is the one that earns the key mark, since it is what makes the subject appear only once.

bullets: T = 2π√(l/g): ÷2π → T/(2π) = √(l/g) → square → T²/(4π²) = l/g → **g = 4π²l/T²** (the reciprocal step is allowed because both sides are single fractions).
Check with T = 2 and l = 1: g = 4π² × 1/4 = π², then T = 2π√(1/π²) = 2π × (1/π) = 2 ✓.
V = (4/3)πr³: multiply by 3 → 3V = 4πr³ → ÷4π → r³ = 3V/(4π) → **r = ∛(3V/(4π))**.
y = √(x² + b): square → y² = x² + b → subtract b → x² = y² − b → **x = ±√(y² − b)**.
Always **square the whole side**: (y − 1)² is y² − 2y + 1, not y² − 1.
A = ½ab sin C, make sin C the subject: sin C = 2A/(ab); this is a link to trigonometry questions.
If asked for the subject in the **Pythagoras formula** c² = a² + b², then a = √(c² − b²) (subtraction **inside** the root).
core.h: Subject inside a root or power with other terms (Higher)
core.p: Some Higher questions combine the ideas above. For example, T = 2π√(l/g) can be rearranged for **g**, which is in the denominator **inside** a square root. The method is to peel off layers in reverse order: first divide by 2π to isolate the root, then square both sides to remove the root, then deal with the fraction. This gives g = 4π²l/T². The skill is simply recognising the layers of the formula and removing them one at a time, always applying each operation to the **whole** side so that nothing is skipped. These questions often come from physics (pendulums, orbits, kinetic energy), so it pays to recognise the standard forms.

bullets: Step 1: **circle the target letter** so you do not lose it in a long formula.
Step 2: clear fractions by multiplying **every** term, and expand brackets.
Step 3: move terms so that the target letter's terms are together on one side (change sign when you move across).
Step 4: if the target appears in two or more terms, **factorise** it out as a common factor.
Step 5: undo remaining operations **in reverse order**: first + and −, then × and ÷, then powers and roots.
Step 6: tidy the final answer (single fraction, no stray brackets) and check with simple numbers.
Show every line of working, as the question often carries one mark per correct step.
core.h: Step-by-step method you can use every time
core.p: Having a fixed routine removes the need to think about where to start. First, **identify** the letter you want to be the subject and underline it. Second, **clear** any fractions by multiplying every term by the denominator, and **expand** any brackets that contain the subject along with other terms. Third, **collect** all terms containing the subject on one side of the equals sign. Fourth, **factorise** if the subject appears in more than one term. Fifth, **undo** the remaining operations in reverse order. Finally, **check** by substitution. Following this order means you can tackle any formula, even one you have never seen.

bullets: Question wording **'make … the subject'** demands the algebraic rearrangement; a numerical answer alone gets 0 marks.
Question wording **'find the value of … when …'** allows either method; substitution first is usually quicker for a single value.
Rearranging first is better when you need to calculate **several values**, for example a table of results.
With **units**, check that all quantities use the same units before substituting (for example metres not centimetres).
Substitute with **brackets** round negative numbers: if x = −3 then x² means (−3)² = 9, not −9.
Keep full calculator values through the working and round only at the end, to the accuracy asked.
Never mix methods halfway through: finish the rearrangement properly, then substitute.
core.p: A question might ask you to **find** a value from a formula rather than rearrange it. You then have a choice: substitute first and solve the resulting equation, or rearrange first and substitute afterwards. Both give the same answer, but the examiner's mark scheme depends on what the question says. If a question says 'make x the subject', you must produce the **rearranged formula**; if it says 'work out the value of x when y = 20', substituting y = 20 and solving is a perfectly valid approach. When many values are to be calculated, rearranging first saves time because you do the algebra once.

bullets: s = d/t → **d = st** and **t = d/s**.
F = ma → **a = F/m** and **m = F/a**.
V = IR → **I = V/R** and **R = V/I**.
V = πr²h → **h = V/(πr²)** and **r = √(V/(πh))**.
Simple interest I = PRT/100 → **P = 100I/(RT)**, **R = 100I/(PT)**.
Pythagoras: c² = a² + b² → **a = √(c² − b²)**; area of trapezium A = ½(a + b)h → **h = 2A/(a + b)**.
core.h: Standard physics and geometry formulae to recognise
core.p: The exam often uses formulae from other subjects, and you are expected to rearrange them without being told how. Recognising the layers quickly makes the work much faster. Many are a product, such as **speed = distance/time**, which can be written s = d/t, then d = st and t = d/s; the 'formula triangle' trick is just an application of multiplication and division inverses. Others involve squares, such as **kinetic energy = ½mv²** and **area of a circle = πr²**. Rather than memorise rearrangements, learn the **method** and apply it, since the formula you meet in the exam may be unfamiliar.

bullets: Substitute **easy numbers** (1, 2, 3, 10) into the original and the final formula; both must match.
Check the **form**: does the final answer still contain the new subject? If so, it is not finished.
Check that **inverse operations** have been used (÷ not ×) by looking at units or sense.
Check that you changed the sign when moving a term across the equals sign.
Check that you divided or multiplied **every term**, including those with several letters.
Take care to leave the answer in **simplest form** with a single fraction line where possible.
Write the checking numbers beside your work if there is space; it shows method but is not required.
core.p: Every rearranged formula can be checked in under a minute, and doing so is the best way to catch errors in a non-calculator exam. Choose **simple numbers** for all but the subject, work out the original subject, then substitute your numbers into the new formula and see if you recover the one you started with. A second check is **dimensional sense**: if a rearrangement of F = ma gives a = Fm, the units would be wrong (N kg is not m/s²). A third check is **limiting cases**: if y = k/x then as x gets bigger y should get smaller, so x = k/y must also give a bigger x when y is smaller, which it does.

bullets: **Graphs**: rearrange 3y − 2x = 6 into y = (2/3)x + 2 to find gradient 2/3 and y-intercept 2.
**Trigonometry**: SOHCAHTOA rearrangements such as opp = hyp × sin θ and hyp = opp/sin θ.
**Density, speed, pressure**: D = M/V, S = D/T, P = F/A and their rearrangements.
**Iteration**: x³ + 4x = 10 can be rearranged to x = ∛(10 − 4x) or x = (10 − x³)/4.
**Circle theorems and similarity**: scale factor formulae need rearranging to find lengths.
**Science**: GCSE Physics (v = u + at, E = ½mv²) and Chemistry (moles = mass/Mr) use the same method.
**Quadratics**: x² = k rearranges to x = ±√k, linking to solving by square roots.
core.p: Rearranging formulae is a core algebra skill used in almost every area of GCSE Mathematics and the sciences. In **trigonometry** you rearrange sin θ = opp/hyp to find a side, and in **Pythagoras** you rearrange to find a shorter side. In **ratio, proportion and rates of change** you rearrange speed, density = mass/volume and pressure = force/area. In **graphs**, rearranging a linear equation into y = mx + c reveals the gradient and intercept. In **algebraic fractions** and **iteration**, rearranging an equation into the form x = f(x) is the first step of an iterative method, so this skill underpins much of the Higher paper.

bullets: '**Make … the subject**' means the letter alone on one side, appearing once.
**2 marks**: one correct inverse step (M1) plus correct answer (A1).
**3–4 marks**: expand/clear fractions (M1), collect terms (M1), factorise (M1), final answer (A1).
Do not use a **calculator** to check an algebraic result unless numbers are given; substitution with easy numbers is quicker.
Leave your answer as a **single fraction** or as sum and difference, not as a messy double-decker fraction.
If the question says 'show that', work towards the given result and finish with it clearly stated.
Accept equivalent forms, but **never leave the subject on both sides**, which loses the final mark.
core.p: These questions usually carry 2 marks for a simple rearrangement and 3 to 5 marks for subject-appears-twice problems. Method marks are awarded for each correct stage even if you slip later, so show every line. A typical 4-mark mark scheme gives M1 for clearing fractions or brackets, M1 for collecting terms, M1 for factorising and A1 for the correct final answer. Write each new line starting with the new subject if possible, and never skip the factorising step, as examiners specifically look for it. If you get stuck, say what you are doing in words beside the line, for instance 'collect x terms'.

exam: **'Make x the subject'** is a Higher and Foundation staple; the final line must show x = (an expression with no x in it).
A 2-mark question typically gives **M1** for one correct inverse step and **A1** for the correct answer.
On 3 to 5 mark questions, the mark scheme usually has separate **method marks** for clearing fractions, collecting terms, factorising and dividing.
Always **show each line of working** underneath the last, with equals signs aligned.
If the subject appears **twice**, mention or show the word 'factorise'; the factorising line usually earns a mark.
For a **root** or **square**, check whether ± is needed and include it if the context does not say the value is positive.
Use **brackets** around numerators like (y − 5)/3 so that the division clearly applies to the whole numerator.
**Check** by substituting easy numbers if time allows; it catches sign errors and reciprocal errors.
Equivalent algebraic forms are accepted, but **ISW** (ignore subsequent working) applies only if the correct answer has not been spoiled.
In a **'show that'** question, never start from the answer; work from the given formula to the required form.

mistakes.r: Divide the whole side: x = (y − 5)/3, using brackets or a single fraction.
mistakes.w: Dividing only one term: y = 3x + 5 → x = y − 5/3

mistakes.r: Multiply by x then divide by y to get x = k/y; the reciprocal changes the positions.
mistakes.w: Writing x = y/k when y = k/x

mistakes.r: Write x = ±√y unless the context says the quantity is positive.
mistakes.w: Forgetting ± when square rooting, e.g. x² = y → x = √y

mistakes.r: Do the inverse: subtract a from both sides, giving x = b − a.
mistakes.w: Not changing sign when moving a term: x + a = b → x = b + a

mistakes.r: Collect the x terms, factorise and divide so x appears only once.
mistakes.w: Stopping with the subject on both sides: x = 2y + x/3

mistakes.r: A root cannot be taken term by term; square root the whole expression.
Only common factors cancel: (x + 3)/3 = x/3 + 1; do not cancel the 3 with part of the top.
mistakes.w: Cancelling terms in a fraction, e.g. (x + 3)/3 = x + 1

mistakes.r: Combine into one fraction first: 1/v = (u − f)/(fu), so v = fu/(u − f).
mistakes.w: Taking the reciprocal term by term: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u → v = f − u

mistakes.r: Divide by the whole bracket: x = (3y + 1)/(y − 2).
mistakes.w: Dividing by a bracket one term at a time: x(y − 2) = 3y + 1 → x = 3y + 1 − 2/y

summary: You must be able to rearrange formulae to change the subject, including formulae with brackets, fractions, squares and roots, and (at Higher tier) formulae where the subject appears twice and must be collected and factorised. This is one of the most-used algebra skills, since it underpins graphs, trigonometry, iteration and every science formula you will meet.

terms.d: The single letter on its own on one side of a formula, with all other terms on the other side.
A rule written with an equals sign that links two or more variables.
Rewrite a formula so that a different variable is on its own on one side.
The operation that undoes another: + and −, × and ÷, squaring and square rooting.
A letter that represents a quantity that can change or take different values.
A collection of terms with no equals sign; it can be simplified but not solved.
A statement that two expressions are equal, true only for certain values of the unknown.
A statement that is true for every value of the variable, written with the sign ≡.
A single part of an expression, such as 3x, −5 or y².
The number multiplying a letter in a term, for example 3 in 3x.
Write an expression as a product by taking out a common factor, such as xy − 2x = x(y − 2).
The bottom of a fraction; a subject in the denominator is brought out by multiplying both sides.
Multiply the numerator of each fraction by the denominator of the other, to remove fractions from a/b = c/d.
A number which, when multiplied by itself, gives the original; x² = 9 has roots +3 and −3.
A number which, when cubed, gives the original; written ∛, with only one real value.
Replace a letter with a given number or expression.
One divided by a number; the reciprocal of x is 1/x.
Whatever you do to one side of an equation you must also do to the other side.

worked.ans: t = (v − u)/a. Check: u = 2, a = 3, t = 4 gives v = 14, and (14 − 2)/3 = 4 ✓.
worked.q: Make t the subject of v = u + at. (2 marks)
steps: Subtract u from both sides: v − u = at (M1).
Divide both sides by a: (v − u)/a = t.
Write with t on the left: t = (v − u)/a.

worked.q: Make x the subject of y = (2x + 1)/(x − 3). (4 marks)
steps: Collect x terms on the left, other terms on the right: xy − 2x = 3y + 1 (M1).

worked.ans: g = 4π²l/T². Check: l = 1, g = π² gives T = 2π × √(1/π²) = 2, and 4π² × 1/2² = π² ✓.
worked.q: T = 2π√(l/g). Make g the subject of the formula. (3 marks)
steps: Rearrange (cross-multiply): g × T² = 4π² × l, so g = 4π²l/T² (A1).
